summary_md:
**No document was read.** The extraction returned 0 characters. A targeted search of `C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research` for "frisch", "kelly", "request" and "codebook" found only four unrelated LobbyView codebooks (clients, issues, network, reports). So this paper has no findings to relate to the system.

Paul's annotation identifies the work as **Frisch & Kelly 2007, House Committee Request Data**. That is a dataset, not an argument. It is generally known as a record of the committee assignments House members asked for, set against the assignments they got. That description comes from general knowledge, not from the codebook, so it is UNVERIFIED (DE-062) and supports no numbers here.

The dataset could matter for one component. The Committee/Influence pillar (40% of the live blend) scores seats with owner-set tiers and multipliers: Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8 and Slightly 0.9, with a subcommittee seat at 1/6 of its parent, plus a Chair/Ranking/Vice ladder (`fec/engine/committee_scores.py:25-36`). It treats a seat as structural CU power and never asks how the member came to hold it. Paul flags a chicken-or-egg problem between partisanship and committee selection. Request data is the standard tool for separating self-selection (members ask for committees that match their interests) from the effect of holding the seat. If a member asked for Financial Services, a high committee score may reflect prior CU interest rather than leverage.

The data would also come with limits. It covers past Congresses, the House only, and freshman or transfer requests. It does not cover the 119th Congress, so it can inform design but cannot be joined to the current roster.

**What Paul should do:** supply the codebook PDF so the extraction can be rerun. Until then this entry should carry no weight in any decision.

bearings.paper_claim: UNVERIFIED and unread: the codebook (0 chars extracted) could not be opened. Paul's annotation names it 'Frisch & Kelly 2007, House Committee Request Data'. From general knowledge only, it records House members' committee-assignment requests next to the assignments they received. No numbers can be quoted.
bearings.system_side: The Committee pillar prices seats as structural CU power. Each seat gets an owner-judgment tier weight: Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8 or Slightly 0.9, with subcommittee seats at 1/6. Leadership multipliers are Chair 3.0 full / 7.5 sub, Ranking 2.0 / 4.5 and Vice 1.0 / 2.0. The score is (Membership + Leadership) / 2. Nothing models why a member sits on the committee: self-selection by prior interest is not separated from leverage conferred by the seat. The pillar feeds Influence at 40% of the composite.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only if the codebook confirms request-vs-assignment fields. Even then the data are historical (not the 119th Congress) and House-only, and they cover new assignments and transfers rather than continuing seats. They could support a design check: whether high committee scores reflect pre-existing interest (selection). They could not be used as a live input or an edge or weight source. Strength is weak until the document is read and a second path reproduces any result (DE-062).

gaps_exposed: The Committee pillar has no selection model. Seat weights treat holding a CU-relevant seat as leverage, with no correction for members who requested that committee because they already held CU-aligned interests. Request-vs-assignment data is the usual way to test this, and Paul's own chicken-or-egg note points to it.

The four-pillar blend has no external check that committee scores carry information beyond prior interest. The open question 'do committee scores predict CU-bill markup or advancement' cannot separate the two effects without a selection instrument.

extraction.year: 2026 (inferred, not stated on the page: the text cites 2026 LDA reports and a projected 2025-2026 cycle)
extraction.venue: None. Unpublished client report addressed to Trey Hawkins and Hannah Benito.
extraction.coverage: Full read of the extract (21 lines, about 10.6k characters, file 0b0cbbaaa98a.txt). The file is plain text, not a PDF, so there is no Paul markup (no highlights, underlines or sticky notes) to extract. The extract contains the abstract, the Crypto section, the Community Banks section and the closing recommendations. The Credit Union, Financial Technologies and Credit Arms sections named in the abstract are not in this file. Line 11 is a "(Insert Graph)" placeholder with no image. Corrected metadata: the year is not printed; 2026 is inferred from the content.
extraction.research_question: Across five financial-services industries (Crypto, Community Banks, Financial Technologies, Credit Arms, Credit Unions), how do campaign giving and lobbying differ in scale, direction and effectiveness, and what should Credit Unions do to gain political traction? The question is stated in the abstract (lines 4-5), not as a formal hypothesis.
extraction.theory: No formal theory is stated. The narrative relies on three informal claims: (1) in politics, attention is the scarce resource and money buys attention (line 12); (2) public visibility of giving signals to peers that lobbying is in vogue (line 9); (3) rising spending draws scrutiny and skepticism, creating a "self-destructive feedback loop" (line 14). None of these is tested.
extraction.data: Sources named: FEC, FDIC, SEC and LDA databases (line 4). The extract gives no sample size, unit of analysis or exact date ranges beyond the election cycles 2021-2022, 2023-2024 and a projected 2025-2026. Quoted items are from press interviews and public statements (Bankman-Fried, Armstrong, Dimon, Lummis, ICBA CEOs). Public-opinion figures (31% oppose, 27% support) are given without a source (line 14). LDA member examples are Zach Nunn, Andy Kim, Young Kim and Bill Huizenga (line 17).
extraction.method: Descriptive. Campaign-finance and lobbying information was "extracted at scale" from the named databases, with percentage changes and shares computed from those extracts, plus qualitative material gathered for narrative (line 4). No model, regression, statistical test or uncertainty estimate appears in the extract.
extraction.identification: None. The report makes no causal identification claims with a design. Causal language such as CLARITY Act push as the "impetus" for the 2025-2026 increase (line 9) is asserted, not tested.
extraction.scope: US federal politics and financial services, election cycles 2021-2026. Population: Crypto and Community Banks industry giving and lobbying, with Credit Unions as the recommendation target. Institution and era: post-2021 crypto political spending and the CLARITY Act debate.

key_findings.finding: Crypto industry spending rose from $1.76M in 2021-2022 to $145.5M in 2023-2024. The report calls this an 8,162.6% increase.
Share of Crypto giving from C-suite donors rose sharply between cycles.
Super PACs take most non-direct-to-candidate giving, which is itself most of industry giving.
key_findings.numbers: Super PACs = 71.9% of non-direct giving; non-direct = 70% of industry giving

key_findings.finding: Fairshake is described as the 2nd largest Super PAC and is entirely funded by crypto.
Projected Crypto spending for the 2025-2026 cycle is above $175M, an off-year increase the report attributes to the CLARITY Act push.
Crypto-backed candidates won most primaries they were backed in.
Crypto outspends key allies by a large factor, which the report says leaves Credit Unions unable to compete if they come into conflict with the industry. The graph meant to show this is missing.
key_findings.numbers: factor of about 100 (stated; no underlying figures given)

key_findings.finding: Public support for Crypto legislation is weak: more Americans oppose than support it.
Community Bank members' LDA activity increased in 2026 reports.
key_findings.numbers: average increase of 20 interactions within the year ("interactions" is undefined in the text)

key_findings.finding: Recommendation 1: raise Credit Union giving 41% over the 2023-2024 baseline.
key_findings.numbers: +41%; $4.3M total giving. The baseline dollar figure is not stated; $4.3M/1.41 implies about $3.05M, a derived number and not in the text.

key_findings.finding: Recommendation 2: Credit Unions should encourage employees and middle management to give to industry trade organizations, framed as command, communication and community.
Recommendation 3: run information campaigns with policymakers and the public on how Credit Unions differ from banks.
Credit Unions risk losing political capital by opposing the CLARITY Act alongside the ABA and Dimon, and the report says the ACU later signaled support.

measures: Campaign contributions in dollars by cycle (FEC)
Share of donations by donor role (C-suite share)
Share of giving by vehicle (Super PAC vs direct-to-candidate)
Primary win count for backed candidates
LDA lobbying interaction counts per member ("interactions" undefined)
Public support and opposition percentages for Crypto legislation
limitations: Stated in the text: none. The report has no limitations section and no methods note.

Observed gap: the $1.76M-to-$145.5M figures imply about an 8,167% increase, not the reported 8,162.6%. The difference is small and may come from rounding in the unrounded totals, but the report does not say.
Observed gap: the abstract promises five industries, but the extract covers only Crypto and Community Banks, with no Credit Union or Credit Arms analysis.
Observed gap: the 'factor of 100' outspending claim and the 'graph' are not backed by any table, figure or source in the extract.
Observed gap: the 'interactions' LDA measure and the 31%/27% public-opinion figures have no definition or source.
Observed gap: no sample, unit, or date range is given for the database extracts, and no uncertainty is reported.

Observed gap: the causal claims (CLARITY Act as the 'impetus', a 'self-destructive feedback loop', and the claim that Armstrong's denial of knowledge is 'doubtful') are the author's judgment, not tested results.

summary_md: Paul's own unpublished client report (to Trey Hawkins and Hannah Benito; year not printed, 2026 inferred) surveys political money in financial services and makes three recommendations to Credit Unions: raise giving 41% over the 2023-2024 baseline to about $4.3M, push employee and middle-management giving to trade groups, and run campaigns that set CUs apart from banks. The extract only covers the Crypto and Community Banks sections. Crypto giving rose from $1.76M (2021-22) to $145.5M (2023-24). The text reports +8,162.6%, but the stated figures give about +8,167%. The C-suite share of that giving went from 69% to 98.8%, and super PACs took 71.9% of non-direct giving, which is itself 70% of the total. A 2025-26 projection of more than $175M would be a midterm-cycle rise, which the report attributes to the CLARITY Act. Crypto-backed candidates won 38 of 40 primaries, and opinion runs 31% oppose to 27% support (no source given). Community-bank member LDA activity rose by an average of 20 interactions. The method is descriptive throughout: no model, no uncertainty, no identification design. Against the system as built, the report matters in three places. (1) Mentat's cycle model applies a symmetric x1.8635 presidential factor to general giving on the midterm step. For a crypto-like industry that projects a large 2025-26 drop, the opposite of the report's projection. (2) The per-member LDA interaction counts look like the bill-roster join that the lobbying lane rejected as circular, and they use LDA as a weight source, which D-021 bars. (3) The super-PAC share and the C-suite share both point to gaps in what Mentat currently splits out. All new analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Crypto industry giving is projected north of 175 million dollars for 2025-2026, versus 145.5 million in 2023-2024, an off-year rise the report calls an outlier and attributes to the CLARITY Act push.

bearings.system_side: Code applies one presidential factor u = 1.8635 to the general_giving measure on both cycle steps (UPLIFT_BOTH_STEPS at giving_forecast.py line 1425; gate at line 1888), so the 2025-26 midterm step is scaled by 1/1.8635, about minus 46 percent. Company PACs keep the fitted phi on the midterm step.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only applies if crypto giving is run through the general_giving measure, which was not checked. The report's 175 million is a projection with no stated method, window or source, so it is a counterexample to test, not evidence.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper line 9 confirmed, including the 175 million projection and the CLARITY attribution. Code description confirmed against the comment block and the gate. 1/1.8635 is about 0.537, so minus 46 percent is correct. The wrong-direction point holds only for the general_giving measure, so the bearing is restricted to that measure.

bearings.paper_claim: Crypto outspends key allies by factors of 100, so credit unions would have no chance in a monetary fight with the industry; the supporting graph is a missing placeholder.
bearings.system_side: The head-to-head pull uses a saturating term (x+1) over (x+1) plus HALFF times rcp, weighted by WM and added to a coalition term WP (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl lines 1096-1105). The dashboard prints the cannot fully offset message only when q is at least 1. The functional form is an assumption and is not validated against outcomes.

The no-chance conclusion is not in the code; the code bounds the monetary term and computes a break-even spend. The bounded pull description is accurate as a statement about the functional form only.

summary_issues: The rounding explanation for the 8,162.6 percent versus about 8,167 percent gap holds: an unrounded base near 1.7609, displayed as 1.76, gives 8,162.6 percent. The report should state the unrounded base.
The summary reads the community-bank 20-interaction figure as lobbying-contact evidence. The report never defines interactions, so the figure should be labeled undefined rather than refuted.
The summary says the per-member LDA counts use LDA as a weight source that D-021 bars. That is an inference from the bill-roster join, not a statement in the report, and should be marked inferred.
The summary places the C-suite framing in the abstract. Abstract line 5 names employee and middle-management giving; C-suite appears only at line 7.

The transfer-graph code_ref is narrowed: fec_beneficiary.R lines 1041-1060 cover seeding only. The Support/Oppose partition is at lines 136-145 and 348. The 89 percent figure counts rows in one sheet (R/export_guards.R line 278), not dollars.
The summary implies the midterm factor applies to crypto-like industries. The code applies it only to the general_giving measure; the measure assignment for crypto was not checked.
The summary states that Fairshake is the 2nd largest super PAC and wholly crypto-funded. Those are the report's claims at line 9, with no date or metric, not verified facts.

The summary omits that the abstract promises five industries but the extract contains only Crypto and Community Banks. Credit Union, Financial Technologies and Credit Arms sections are absent from this file.
The summary's descriptions of a self-destructive feedback loop and money buying attention are author judgments with no test, not findings.
The 4.3 million credit union target and its implied baseline of about 3.05 million are derived by the analyst and do not appear in the text. Flag as derived, not reported.
The extract has no Paul markup (no highlights or notes), so Paul-note items are none; coverage is the full 21-line extract.
gaps_exposed: No industry-specific regime-shift term in the cycle model: a bill-driven midterm surge (crypto 2025-26) is forecast as a symmetric midterm drop under the general-giving factor.
Mentat produces no occupation-role (C-suite vs employee) split of individual giving, which the report's main CU recommendation depends on.
The support/oppose attributed-estimate producer for super-PAC money is unbuilt, so super-PAC share of industry giving cannot yet be read as support for candidates.
No primary-election outcome measure exists to test claims like 38 of 40 backed primaries won.
No independent member-level lobbying contact measure exists; per-member LDA counts can only come from the circular bill-roster join.
flags: D-021 and refuted lobbied-member link: per-member LDA interaction counts (average +20) use LDA as a member weight and, if from the bill-roster join, are circular by construction; do not cite as lobbying contact.

Window and denominator missing: factor of 100 outspending, average of 20 interactions (which members, which baseline year), 38 of 40 primaries (which cycles), 31% vs 27% opinion (no source), Fairshake rank 2 (no date or metric).
Arithmetic: $1.76M to $145.5M is about +8,167%, not the reported +8,162.6% (likely rounding of unrounded totals; unstated).
Causal and influence language without a design: CLARITY Act as the impetus, money buys attention, self-destructive feedback loop; all asserted, untested.
Coverage: abstract promises five industries but the extract contains only Crypto and Community Banks; the CU baseline dollar figure is not stated ($4.3M / 1.41 implies about $3.05M, derived).
Any agent recomputation here is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: No bibliography entries; this is Paul's own report. Its focus on employee giving and CU distinctiveness fits the built 16-PAC CU cohort. Two claims are stale against the system: the per-member LDA interaction counts rest on the bill-roster link the lobbying lane refuted as circular (and D-021 bars LDA as a weight), and the midterm crypto surge clashes with Mentat's symmetric general-giving midterm factor (D-121), which forecasts a decline. Money-buys-attention is untested here.

Furnas, LaPira and Brock find low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which bears on the report's implicit reading of LDA activity and giving as one push. The report does not state that reading, so this is not a direct contradiction. Relation changed from contradicts to complements.
Randomized field experiment on contributions and access; the nearest tested version of the report's money-buys-attention claim, which the report leaves untested. Use access wording, not influence.
LobbyView bill-level LDA data is the likely source of the bill-roster join behind the per-member counts. The report does not name its source, so this link is inferred.
Work on dynamics of the US lobbying network, relevant to the cycle-phase assumption. Its cycle-synchronization claim was not checked against the Bacik text here.

meta.venue: Research note, Georgetown University affiliation, dated September 24, 2026, addressed to an advisor

extraction.title: Request for Review: Industry Economic Performance and Political Spending
extraction.venue: Research note, Georgetown University affiliation, dated September 24, 2026, addressed to an advisor
extraction.document_type: Internal research design note requesting review; no models estimated yet
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (18,889 chars, 282 lines): all sections 1-10 and data links. Lobbying, elections and projected control, legislators (committee jurisdiction) and sector allocation are covered in Sections 4-8. Networks, path-finding, persuasion/turnout and text measurement are not discussed. No annotation files exist (annot_sha12s is empty), so paul_markup is empty and 0 items were dropped. Text-only; no page images. Author treated as Paul because p.note is true. Metadata hints checked: title, author and year 2026 are correct; venue and document type are corrected here.
extraction.research_question: Does a U.S. industry's year-over-year economic performance predict how much it spends on federal politics, through campaign contributions and through lobbying? How does expected partisan control of Congress shape both the amount and the partisan direction of that spending?
extraction.theory: Competing accounts: deep pockets (H1, better years mean more spending); distress (H1-alt, bad years mean more lobbying for relief, as in 2008-09 bailouts); access-seeking (H2, contributions shift toward the party expected to hold the majority); stakes (H3, total contributions rise when a chamber is a toss-up); lobbying tracks current power (H4). Majority status is treated as worth access (committee chairs, agenda control), citing Cox and Magar 1999. Section 8 cites Grier, Munger and Roberts 1994 on potential government benefits and collective-action limits.
extraction.data: Five initial sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto (crypto analyzed separately). Unit: sector by year, with sector by chamber by year for RShare. Proposed period 2008-2025, annual; extension to 1998 possible. About 9 elections in sample, six of which flipped a chamber (House 2010, 2018, 2022; Senate 2014, 2020, 2024). Sources: OpenSecrets bulk data, DIME v4.0 (1979-2024), FEC bulk data, OpenSecrets lobbying, LDA.gov API (quarterly LD-2 since 2008), Iowa Electronic Markets, Cook Political Report ratings (1984-present), 538 generic-ballot averages (back to 1996), FRED. N is not stated; the text implies about 18 observations per sector, roughly 90 sector-years (computed here, not stated).
extraction.method: Pooled panel with sector fixed effects, not per-sector regressions. (1) log contributions on prior-year growth, same-year growth, negative-growth dummy, Midterm, Pres, Tossup, trend. (2) RShare by chamber on growth, Shift, RMajNow, Midterm, Pres. (3) log lobbying on lagged log lobbying, growth, Neg, Unified, Midterm, Pres, sample from 2008. Growth is real, z-scored within sector. Robustness: year fixed effects; Shift x RLean; expected seat change. Inference: wild cluster bootstrap by sector; Driscoll-Kraay where year-level terms enter. Forecasts are used only after estimation, to predict 2026.
extraction.identification: No causal claims (Section 7). Prior-year growth is the main test because same-year growth may be caused by the spending and early-year money precedes most growth (Section 4.1). Sector fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences. Year fixed effects give the cleanest growth test but absorb projected control. Projected control rests on about 9 elections; Shift x RLean adds sector-by-year variation. Lobbying uses current control (unified vs divided) because lobbyists work on the sitting Congress.
extraction.scope: Federal campaign contributions and federal lobbying (LDA) only. Five sectors, possibly expanded to every BEA industry matchable to OpenSecrets codes (about 70 BEA industries). Era 2008-2025 proposed, with possible extension to 1998. Life insurance is mainly state-regulated (McCarran-Ferguson), so federal-only scope is an open question (Section 8D). Fairshake outside spending is not candidate contributions.

key_findings.finding: No models estimated yet; the note reports design decisions only, with no empirical results.
Projected control is measured as probability of majority, not raw expected seat gains; seat change kept as robustness check.
Prior-year growth is the main test; same-year growth is secondary because it can be caused by the spending itself.
Cook Political Report final ratings (1984-2022) were correct about 94 percent of the time for Lean, 97 percent for Likely, about 100 percent for Solid.
Cox and Magar (1999) estimate House majority status worth about 36,000 dollars per member in corporate and trade PAC receipts around the 1994 switch; cited in the note, not verified.
Only about 9 elections in the sample; six flipped one chamber.
Fairshake super PAC raised roughly 260 million dollars over 2023-24, mostly from a handful of firms and founders; outside spending, not contributions.
OpenSecrets API was discontinued April 15, 2025; bulk data remain free for non-commercial use.

measures: Contrib: sector contributions by calendar year, CPI-deflated, summed by transaction date
RShare: Republican share of the sector's two-party contributions to chamber c candidates
Lobby: reported federal lobbying spending, CPI-deflated
G: real year-over-year growth, z-scored within sector; Neg: 1 if prior-year growth negative
P: probability Republicans hold chamber c after next election, measured before the money is given
Shift = P minus RMajNow; Tossup = 1 minus absolute value of (2P minus 1)
RLean: sector average Republican share over the sample
Pres and Midterm dummies (odd years baseline); Unified control

Growth candidates: bank assets and net income (FDIC); credit union assets, loans, membership (NCUA); life premiums and assets (ACLI, NAIC, BEA); auto real value added (BEA) and industrial production (Fed G.17); crypto market cap (CoinGecko, Coin Metrics)
limitations: Few elections (about 9); projected-control estimates rest on few independent observations (Section 7)
Few sectors (5 clusters) make inference fragile; wild cluster bootstrap proposed (Sections 5, 7)
Reverse causality for same-year growth (Section 7)
Growth measures not comparable across sectors (Section 7)
OpenSecrets codes do not match NAICS; BEA combines banks with credit unions and life insurers with other carriers (Section 7)
Regime changes: Citizens United and SpeechNow (2010), McCutcheon (2014), 2008 LDA reporting change, CUNA and NAFCU merger effective January 1, 2024 (Section 7)
Crypto: short history and very concentrated donors (Section 7)
Unobserved spending: 501(c) dark money and unregistered lobbying (Section 7)
Correlational design; no causal claims (Section 7)
Post-2007-08 drop in registered lobbyists, possibly shadow lobbying (Section 8C.8)
Odd-year prediction markets often not open, so P is hard to measure in odd years (Section 8B.5)
Open question whether 5 to 10 sectors allow reliable inference (Section 8E.13)

short_quotes.quote: Growth is correlated from year to year, so separate models would each pick up part of the other's effect.
Access comes with majority status: committee chairs and control of the agenda.
Actual election results would be hindsight, and they are partly caused by the money.

summary_md: Paul's September 24, 2026 design memo to a secondary advisor (Astra) asks whether a sector's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal campaign giving and lobbying, and how expected partisan control shapes the amount and direction of that money. It reports no estimates. It sets out five hypotheses (deep pockets, distress, access-seeking, stakes, lobbying tracks current power) and three pooled sector fixed-effects models. Model 1 is log contributions on prior- and same-year growth together (a distributed lag), a negative-growth dummy, Midterm/Pres, a Tossup term and a trend. Model 2 is Republican two-party share on Shift = P minus RMajNow. Model 3 is log lobbying with a lagged dependent variable and Unified control. Inference is a wild sector-cluster bootstrap with Driscoll-Kraay errors. The proposed panel is 2008-2025 with five sectors, about 9 elections and 6 chamber flips. The memo is the method source for the Mentat sector growth study, and the Codex ORIGINAL_MODEL_CONTRACT transcribes it. The R build diverges from it. Each growth timing enters its own model (C1/C2/C3) rather than one distributed lag. Totals carry a signed exp_dem control where the memo calls for Tossup. There is no negative-growth dummy, trend or lagged lobbying term. The primary window is 2020-2025 (three elections), not 2008-2025. Results so far are null or fragile: no stable partisan shift (-0.04, p .76), and the lobbying growth lead flips sign under year FE. The memo's leverage worries therefore apply to the build with more force. The only within-cycle access-seeking signal, SEATS-W (-3.47 pp per expected D seat, House 2022), comes from one election and uses expected seats, the measure the memo demoted to a robustness check. All agent readings here are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Pooled sector-FE models: (1) log Contrib on G(t-1), G(t), Neg(t-1), Midterm, Pres, Tossup, Trend; (2) RShare by chamber on growth, Shift, RMajNow, Midterm, Pres; (3) log Lobby on lagged log Lobby, growth, Neg, Unified. Growth z-scored within sector; CPI-deflated dollars; wild cluster bootstrap by sector; proposed sample 2008-2025 with 5 initial sectors (expansion to about 70 BEA industries allowed).
bearings.system_side: sgs_registry.R builds C1-C3 and L1-L3 as sector-FE tests with wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector (Webb six-point weights); sgs_estimate.R header confirms this inference. Growth z-scoring and log DVs not checked in code here (the registry default DV is levels; see next bearing).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only as a statement of the memo design. The build departs from it (next bearing), so build results must not be read as memo tests.

Memo model 2 also includes Midterm and Pres, which the rel omits. Code lines confirmed: C and L loops at registry 112-120; WCR with Webb six-point weights at estimate.R 1-10.

bearings.paper_claim: Both growth timings belong in one regression (distributed lag) because separate models would each pick up part of the other effect. Totals get Tossup = 1 - abs(2P - 1), not a signed Republican-gains term. A Neg dummy, a Trend and lagged log lobbying are included. Lobbying uses Unified control.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.1 items 1, 7 and 8; Section 4.3; Section 5 equations 1 and 3
bearings.system_side: Registry runs C1, C2 and C3 as separate single-growth models, not jointly. Contribution controls are pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate; the core has no Tossup, Neg or Trend term. Lobbying adds cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate and has no lagged DV. Contribution DV defaults to real dollar levels (contributions_real_m), with logs only in robustness. Primary window 2020-2025 (R8). The g_pos/g_neg asymmetry split is an EXTENSION family from the 2026-09-26 rulings, not the core spec, so the rel statement that decline years use it as the core is softened. The expected-control terms are not P in levels: per year they come from an IEM annual mean, a binary forecaster final call (Democrats at or above 218 House or 51 Senate seats), or a market snapshot. The 2023 value is a final call flagged as measured Nov 2024, after the year.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies to every CORE C and L result. Rulings R4-R8 and the 2026-09-26 rulings may supersede parts of the memo, but results from separate-timing, signed-control models should not be reported as tests of memo H1 or H3.
bearings.verifier_note: Memo text (Section 4.1 items 1, 7, 8; 4.3; equations 1 and 3) confirmed. Code confirms separate C1-C3, no core Neg, Trend, Tossup or lagged DV, and window 2020-2025. Softened: ASYM is an extension family, and exp_dem is a per-year method mix (including a 0/1 call measured after the year), not P levels as the rel summary says.

bearings.paper_claim: Probability of majority control is the preferred projected-control measure because access comes with majority status (Cox and Magar 1999, about 36,000 USD per member, cited and not verified here). Expected seat change is kept only as a robustness check. Q4 asks how quickly PAC giving tracks changing expectations within a cycle; Q7 asks about an event study around expected flips.
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W is a weekly test in report 221444: 17 weeks, 2022 House only (2020 and 2024 not usable yet). Dependent variable is the Democratic share of gross positive receipts. Regressor is the prior-week change in 538 Lite expected Democratic seats, with a week-of-cycle trend. House level, pooled-dollar (the first row of the primary table): -3.36 pp per seat, block-bootstrap p 0.11 and 0.10, not significant. The -3.47 pp figure with p 0.0086 and 0.0174 (Holm 0.034 and 0.070) is the equal-sector variant. Senate level is null in both weightings (equal-sector +6.23, p 0.65; pooled-dollar +3.99, p 0.81).

bearings.paper_claim: Election-cycle controls use Pres and Midterm dummies with odd years as the baseline. Industry forecasts (IBISWorld, trade outlooks) are used only to predict 2026 spending after estimation and are never mixed into the estimated growth variable.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.2 (cycle controls); Section 4.1 item 6 (forecasts used only at prediction)
bearings.system_side: The cycle model projects with M = B exp(phi dP + d_h) (1 + x/2), where dP = Pres(c) minus Pres(c-2) is a presidential-cycle difference, not a Midterm dummy with odd-year baseline. The IBISWorld real growth path, lagged one year, enters only through the projection term x. Forecast growth is kept out of estimation in this model. The sector study does put predicted_growth_pct on the right-hand side in C3 and L3 (sgs_registry.R:30), which the memo prohibits; that departure is outside this bearing.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports only the forecast product split between estimation and projection. Does not cover the sector study C3 and L3 tests, and the presidential-difference term is not the memo Midterm and Pres dummy set.

summary_issues: SEATS-W headline -3.47 pp (p 0.0086 and 0.0174) is the equal-sector variant. The pooled-dollar primary row is -3.36 pp with p 0.11 and 0.10 and is not significant. The rel does not say which weighting it reports.
SEATS-W regressor is the prior-week change in 538 Lite expected Democratic seats with a week-of-cycle trend, not the level of expected seats as the summary states.

The no-stable-shift figure (-0.04, p 0.76) is the SHIFT-Chamber-PV preview: 80 rows, 4 residual df, below the 6-year minimum. Core SHIFT-Chamber and SHIFT-House are NOT ESTIMABLE in report 221444 (5 of 6 years). The SATURATED at 2 years wording does not match that report.

Majority probability P is not what enters as exp_dem levels. The panel uses per-year IEM annual means, a binary forecaster final call (Democrats at or above 218 House or 51 Senate seats), or a market snapshot. The 2023 value is a final call measured Nov 2024, after the year, which departs from the memo measured-before-money rule (Section 4.3). The rel does not record this.
L3-LV year-FE coefficient -0.4765 (rel -0.477) is not significant (p 0.15, CI -1.02 to 0.73). The rel presents the sign flip without that qualifier.

The within-cycle signal claim is overstated: equal-sector House lag (-3.05, p 0.014) and 538 Classic equal-sector level (-3.59, p 0.036) are also negative. All rest on one cycle, as the report itself says.

Related link anon-2025-cross-industry-political is not same-data. The memo covers executive and CEO giving for the top ten firms by revenue in four industries and has no lobbying measure. Dropped from related.
Imai and Kim (2021) text has no discussion of lagged dependent variables with fixed effects; the rel attribution is unsupported and was removed.
The ORIGINAL_MODEL_CONTRACT note and its transcription claim were not located in the sector_growth_study folder. Unverified.
Confirmed by absence in code/R: no Tossup, Driscoll-Kraay or Shift x RLean term in the registry tests. Not checked: the paul_alignment claim that growth adds no adjusted R2.
Coverage: all 4 bearings and all 9 related links checked; 8 kept, 1 dropped. Text-only review; page images not available.
gaps_exposed: No distributed-lag core model: the build never enters G(t-1) and G(t) jointly in one regression, which the memo's main argument (Section 4.1 item 1) requires; C1 and C2 each risk absorbing the other's effect.
No Tossup (stakes, H3) term exists anywhere in the R study code; contribution totals carry signed exp_dem controls, which the memo argues against for total-dollar outcomes.

Lobbying models lack the lagged dependent variable the memo specifies (Kerr et al. persistence), and the memo's open question Q13 on Nickell bias with FE plus a lagged DV over about 18 years is unaddressed.
Driscoll-Kraay errors for year-level terms are not implemented; the build uses two-way cluster SE as its sensitivity check instead (contract: neither may be silently replaced).
The primary window of 2020-2025 gives about 3 elections against the memo's 9, so the projected-control leverage the memo already calls weak is thinner still; SHIFT House is SATURATED at 2 years.
The Shift x RLean interaction, which the memo calls the stronger test because it survives year FE, is not among the registry tests located here.
Majority probability P is used as exp_dem levels; the memo's Shift = P - RMajNow appears only as the derived exp_shift reparametrisation, not as the primary SHIFT focal term.

C3/L3 regress spending on IBISWorld predicted growth in estimation, contrary to the memo's rule that forecasts never enter the growth variable; this is ruled (R6) but not labelled as a departure from the memo.
flags: Pooled coefficients across sectors with incomparable growth sources (crypto market cap vs bank assets) cross a known fault line; quote them with per-sector strata (the SLOPES family) or label them UNSTRATIFIED.

Every figure from the build must name its window (2020-2025 primary, 2021-2025 preview, 2022-only SEATS-W) and its denominator (sector-years or unit-weeks); the memo's 2008-2025 framing does not describe the built results.
Cox and Magar's 36,000 USD per member figure and Cook's 94/97/100 percent accuracy figures are cited and were not verified against sources on disk.

LDA spending as a dependent variable is consistent with D-021, since it is not an edge or weight; the memo's issue-code alternative (Q8) would still be a measurement choice and must not become a member-level lobbying edge.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals or the reciprocity rule; the memo does not touch networks.
This reading is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: No annotations; this is Paul own design memo. Evidence so far does not back his deep-pockets or access-seeking hypotheses: growth adds no adjusted R2, L3-LV +0.352 flips to -0.477 under sector plus year FE, SHIFT shows no stable partisan move (-0.04, p .76), matching the memo own caution (no causal claims, few elections, 5 clusters). The memo is stale against the build: window moved to a 2020-2025 primary (R8), scope grew to nine sectors, and joint timings, Tossup, Neg, lagged lobbying and Driscoll-Kraay are not what the R registry runs.

related.why: Imai and Kim (2021) on two-way fixed effects for causal inference supports caution about the memo year FE plan. The text has no lagged-dependent-variable discussion, so the rel attribution about a lagged DV with few units is not carried over.

Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters (2020) find interest-group donations directly tied to subsequent lobbying, supporting separate modeling of giving and lobbying. The unit is interest group, not firm as the rel says.
Finds minimal overlap between organizations that lobby and organizations making campaign expenditures. Bears on memo questions 2 and 8.
Partisan ties with the House majority party are valued by clients, and the paper tests firm value around the 2011 change in House control. Relevant to the access-with-majority logic in H2 and H4.
Estimates firm-level returns to lobbying (abstract and counterfactuals). Relevant to the deep-pockets reading; the link to H1 is interpretive.
Introduces the common-space CFscores that DIME uses for the RShare outcome.
Reports lobbying network dynamics with periodicity synchronized with the presidential election cycle, supporting the memo Pres and Midterm controls in the lobbying model.
Covers Fairshake and the concentrated crypto lobby, supporting the memo choice to analyze crypto separately.
Paul earlier report on five financial sectors using FEC, FDIC, SEC and LDA data. Overlapping sectors and sources, but a snapshot report, not the sector-year panel.
